content.text: is there a way through the git cli to only fetch by blob hash?
I’m checking the Git docs to answer this precisely, since object transport details are easy to misstate.

Not with normal `git fetch`.

The closest options are:

- `partial clone` / promisor remotes: Git can lazily fetch a missing blob when some command needs it, but that is demand-driven, not a user-facing `git fetch <blobhash>` command.
- Low-level `git fetch-pack`: it can request a raw 40-hex object ID if the server allows `uploadpack.allowTipSHA1InWant`, `uploadpack.allowReachableSHA1InWant`, or `uploadpack.allowAnySHA1InWant`. That is not blob-specific in the UX, and Git may still download dependent/referenced objects rather than only that one blob.

So the practical answer is: no clean high-level Git CLI command exists to “fetch only this blob by hash”. If you’re working with partial clones, Git can fetch missing blobs on demand; otherwise you’re into low-level `fetch-pack` territory and server support matters.

Sources:
- `git-fetch-pack`: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-fetch-pack
- `partial-clone`: https://git-scm.com/docs/partial-clone

> GitHub's git protocol doesn't honor blob SHAs in `want` lines (only commit SHAs reachable from refs), so `git fetch <url> <blob-sha>` always fails

is this sentence making any sense?
I’m verifying the GitHub-specific part, because the Git protocol rules and GitHub’s server policy are separate claims.

It mostly makes sense, but it’s imprecise in two places.

A tighter version would be:

> GitHub’s `upload-pack` does not appear to support arbitrary object-ID fetches by SHA via the normal Git fetch protocol, so `git fetch <url> <blob-sha>` fails. `git fetch` normally expects refs, and raw SHA fetches only work when the server explicitly allows them.

Why I’d change it:

- `git fetch <url> <blob-sha>` is not really “fetch by blob hash” syntax in a guaranteed sense. The second argument is normally a ref/refspec, not “an object ID”.
- “only commit SHAs reachable from refs” is too specific and probably misleading. In Git’s lower-level docs, raw 40-hex object IDs can be accepted if the server enables certain `uploadpack.allow*SHA1InWant` options; that behavior is server policy, not a universal protocol rule, and it is not blob-specific in the client syntax.
- I couldn’t find official GitHub docs explicitly saying “GitHub rejects blob SHA wants”; that part sounds like an inference from observed behavior, not a documented guarantee.

If you want a one-sentence version that is both accurate and conservative:

> `git fetch <url> <blob-sha>` fails on GitHub because `git fetch` expects refs unless the server permits raw object-ID wants, and GitHub does not appear to expose that for arbitrary blob objects.

Sources:
- `git-fetch-pack`: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-fetch-pack
- `partial-clone`: https://git-scm.com/docs/partial-clone
- GitHub blob API, showing GitHub supports blob lookup via API even if not via `git fetch`: https://docs.github.com/en/rest/git/blobs
does any forge allow this?
I’m checking documented server behavior rather than guessing from anecdote.

Yes, at least GitLab appears to.

What I could verify:

- Git’s low-level `fetch-pack` supports raw 40-hex object IDs if the server enables `uploadpack.allowTipSHA1InWant`, `uploadpack.allowReachableSHA1InWant`, or `uploadpack.allowAnySHA1InWant`. Source: `git-fetch-pack` docs.  
  https://git-scm.com/docs/git-fetch-pack
- GitLab enabled `uploadpack.allowAnySHA1InWant` by default in GitLab 13.2 for Gitaly, specifically so clients could fetch by SHA without creating persistent refs. Source: GitLab MR discussion.  
  https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/81066
- GitLab also has older work showing `allowAnySHA1InWant` being wired into `upload-pack`.  
  https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/16850

The important caveat is wording:

- For GitLab, I found evidence for “fetch any SHA” support.
- I did not find a GitLab doc that explicitly says “blob SHA fetches are supported,” but `allowAnySHA1InWant` is an arbitrary object-ID setting, so blob support is a reasonable inference from Git’s server semantics.

For other forges:

- Gerrit: I found docs for enabling fetch-by-commit-ID when refs are hidden via `uploadpack.allowTipSha1InWant`, but that is narrower and commit-focused.  
  https://gerrit-review.googlesource.com/Documentation/config-gerrit.html
- GitHub: I did not find evidence that its Git transport allows arbitrary object-ID fetches.
- Self-hosted forges generally can, if they expose/configure the underlying `upload-pack` options.

So the short answer is: yes, GitLab does, and self-hosted Git servers/forges can if they enable the relevant `upload-pack` settings.
can you give me a command with which I could test this against GitHub?

Use `git fetch-pack`, not `git fetch`, so you test raw object-ID wants directly:

```bash
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d) &&
git -C "$tmpdir" init -q &&
git -C "$tmpdir" fetch-pack -v https://github.com/OWNER/REPO.git BLOB_SHA
```

Replace `OWNER/REPO` and `BLOB_SHA` with a full 40-hex blob ID.

If GitHub rejects it, you should see an error along the lines of:

```text
error: Server does not allow request for unadvertised object
```

If you want packet-level proof of what the server advertised and rejected:

```bash
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d) &&
git -C "$tmpdir" init -q &&
GIT_TRACE_PACKET=1 git -C "$tmpdir" fetch-pack -v https://github.com/OWNER/REPO.git BLOB_SHA
```

For a control test, run the same command against a branch-tip commit SHA from that repo. If the server allows that case but not the blob, the difference will be clear.
can you give me an example for the local git repo, that I can try this with real data?
I’m pulling a real blob ID from this repo so the example is runnable as-is.

Yes. Using this repo, here’s a real example with a real blob SHA from `HEAD`:

```bash
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d) &&
git -C "$tmpdir" init -q &&
git -C "$tmpdir" fetch-pack -v /Users/soph/Work/entire/devenv/cli_experiments 228bfe60a76e39a2d85e43259d2440ddb2f6bada
```

That blob SHA is for `.allowed-licenses` in this repo.

For a control, test a real commit SHA from the same repo:

```bash
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d) &&
git -C "$tmpdir" init -q &&
git -C "$tmpdir" fetch-pack -v /Users/soph/Work/entire/devenv/cli_experiments $(git -C /Users/soph/Work/entire/devenv/cli_experiments rev-parse HEAD)
```

If you want the packet trace too:

```bash
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d) &&
git -C "$tmpdir" init -q &&
GIT_TRACE_PACKET=1 git -C "$tmpdir" fetch-pack -v /Users/soph/Work/entire/devenv/cli_experiments 228bfe60a76e39a2d85e43259d2440ddb2f6bada
```

If you want, I can also give you the same test against this repo’s `origin` remote with a real blob SHA from a public GitHub repo.

  git -C "$tmpdir" init -q &&
  git -C "$tmpdir" fetch-pack -v /Users/soph/Work/entire/devenv/cli_experiments 228bfe60a76e39a2d85e43259d2440ddb2f6bada

Right, that succeeded because `/Users/soph/Work/entire/devenv/cli_experiments` is a local repository path, not a hosted forge.

That test proves `git fetch-pack` can request an object ID directly. It does not prove anything about GitHub, because with a local repo there is no forge policy layer deciding whether unadvertised object wants are allowed.

If you want a GitHub-specific test, use the same blob SHA against the repo’s GitHub URL:

```bash
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d) &&
git -C "$tmpdir" init -q &&
git -C "$tmpdir" fetch-pack -v https://github.com/entireio/cli.git 228bfe60a76e39a2d85e43259d2440ddb2f6bada
```

If you want packet trace too:

```bash
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d) &&
git -C "$tmpdir" init -q &&
GIT_TRACE_PACKET=1 git -C "$tmpdir" fetch-pack -v https://github.com/entireio/cli.git 228bfe60a76e39a2d85e43259d2440ddb2f6bada
```

Expected interpretation:

- If it succeeds, GitHub allowed that object-ID want.
- If it fails with something like `Server does not allow request for unadvertised object`, GitHub rejected it.

So the correction is: your local test validated the client-side mechanism, not GitHub’s server behavior.

❯   tmpdir=$(mktemp -d) &&
  git -C "$tmpdir" init -q &&
  git -C "$tmpdir" fetch-pack -v https://github.com/entireio/cli.git 228bfe60a76e39a2d85e43259d2440ddb2f6bada
fatal: protocol 'https' is not supported

That failure is unrelated to blob fetching. It means your Git installation cannot use the HTTPS transport in this environment.

Use one of these instead:

```bash
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d) &&
git -C "$tmpdir" init -q &&
git -C "$tmpdir" fetch-pack -v git@github.com:entireio/cli.git 228bfe60a76e39a2d85e43259d2440ddb2f6bada
```

Or, if your local repo already has `origin` set to a working transport, reuse it:

```bash
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d) &&
git -C "$tmpdir" init -q &&
git -C "$tmpdir" fetch-pack -v "$(git -C /Users/soph/Work/entire/devenv/cli_experiments remote get-url origin)" 228bfe60a76e39a2d85e43259d2440ddb2f6bada
```

If you want to confirm the transport issue first:

```bash
git remote-https -h
```

If that says command not found or similar, your Git was built/installed without the HTTPS helper on `PATH`.

So the test you want is still `fetch-pack`; you just need to run it over a transport your Git supports, usually SSH.

  git -C "$tmpdir" init -q &&
  git -C "$tmpdir" fetch-pack -v git@github.com:entireio/cli.git 228bfe60a76e39a2d85e43259d2440ddb2f6bada

Then the earlier claim was wrong, at least for this case.

Your command shows GitHub did honor a raw blob object ID in a `want` line and returned exactly that blob. So this sentence is not accurate:

> GitHub's git protocol doesn't honor blob SHAs in `want` lines

A better statement is:

> GitHub can serve at least some blob objects by raw SHA via `git fetch-pack`; `git fetch <url> <sha>` is the wrong test because `git fetch` expects refs/refspecs, while `fetch-pack` directly exercises object-ID wants.

The likely nuance is:

- `git fetch` and `git fetch-pack` are not equivalent tests.
- GitHub may allow reachable object-ID wants via `upload-pack`.
- Your successful result is concrete evidence that blob-by-SHA is possible on GitHub over SSH for that repository/object.

So if your goal is to test “can this forge serve a blob by object ID?”, `fetch-pack` is the right probe, and GitHub passed it here.
